newsitem.title: UK: North Brazil sugar prices seen steady to year-end.
newsitem.headline: North Brazil sugar prices seen steady to year-end.

text.p: Raw sugar prices from north Brazil's bumper cane crop should be supported towards the end of the year as the hefty U.S. import quota drags competitive central American sugars northwards, brokers said on Friday.

Although north Brazil premiums have fallen to around 20/25 points over New York's spot October contract from 35/40 points recently, the quota is expected to reduce western hemisphere raws availability and balance the expected increase in output.
"The central Americans this year seem to have been scooped up by the U.S. quota," said one broker.
"Although it's slightly down on last year it looks as if there is going to be a pretty good U.S. quota. It's going to be quite tight," he said.

The U.S. Agriculture Department recently set the sugar import quota for the 1997 fiscal year at 2.3 million tonnes, with 1.7 million tonnes to be allocated immediately and the rest hinging on reviews set for January, March and May.

Brazil, along with the Philippines and the Dominican Republic, are to receive quota certificates allowing them to ship up to 25 percent of their quota during each quarter, and unentered allocations may be carried into other quarters.
The three producers are the largest quota holders among three or four dozen nations.
The U.S. requirement will take advantage of the expected production increase in north Brazil, which brokers said was probably the only origin to be delivered against New York's October contract.

Trade sources said while it was still too early to gauge the exact size of the north Brazilian crop, a total cane crush of 48.5 million tonnes is expected, producing 3.35 million tonnes of sugar and 1.75 million in exports.
"One never knows with Brazil how much will actually come out, with the requirements for domestic (needs) and alcohol," said one physical sugar trader.
However, in its latest report Czarnikow Sugar said north Brazil could set a new sugar production record in 1996/97, exceeding last year's record of 3.54 million tonnes raw value.
Exports from the region could soar once the government finally removed a 40-percent tax on the remaining 20 percent of permitted sugar exports, it said.
Some brokers suggested that South Africa's bumper crop could compete with north Brazil as the country is well placed geographically to supply raws to both west and east hemispheres.
But others said South African sugar was unlikely to be delivered against October and availability would be limited at best for the remainder of the year.
"The South Africans are getting towards the end of their season so they certainly won't be involved in the tape," said one London trader.
Although north Brazil's crop will be mainly raw sugar, most of the small amount of 45 ICUMSA whites is said to have been bought in advance by European trade houses.
"There's probably between 400,000 and 500,000 tonnes available and most is already sold," said another trader.
Cargoes of North Brazil whites were quoted at a $5/7 discount for December/January, while October/November cargoes were offered at a $8 discount, market sources said.
